Lecture 17

Contour integration and Cauchy’s formulas

Lecture objectives

We define paths and contour integrals and evaluate them with antiderivatives. We prove Cauchy’s theorem for analytic functions with a continuous derivative, on regions where Green’s theorem applies, and deduce the deformation of paths and Cauchy’s integral and derivative formulas. We prove that every nonconstant polynomial has a root. With Goursat’s theorem, which we cite, the continuity hypothesis can be dropped, and every analytic function has derivatives of every order.

Lecture 16 counted the turns of a closed path around a point. We now integrate analytic functions along paths, and this winding number becomes an integral. For a function analytic on an open set containing a region, the Cauchy–Riemann equations make its integral around the boundary vanish, and Cauchy’s formulas recover the function and its derivatives inside a circle from its values on it. The lecture reads in three stages: paths, contour integrals and antiderivatives (Sections 17.1–17.2), Cauchy’s theorem and integral formula (Sections 17.3–17.4), and derivatives of every order and paths through a singular point (Sections 17.5–17.6).

17.3 Cauchy’s theorem

Cauchy’s theorem comes from Green’s theorem. We recall the regions of GM 40, and we keep its letter DDD for them. A compact region DDD is simple in both directions if D={a≤x≤b, g1(x)≤y≤g2(x)}={c≤y≤d, h1(y)≤x≤h2(y)}D=\{a\le x\le b,\ g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\}=\{c\le y\le d,\ h_1(y)\le x\le h_2(y)\}D={a≤x≤b, g1​(x)≤y≤g2​(x)}={c≤y≤d, h1​(y)≤x≤h2​(y)} with continuous functions g1≤g2g_1\le g_2g1​≤g2​ and h1≤h2h_1\le h_2h1​≤h2​ that are piecewise C1,C^1C1, except that a one-sided slope may be infinite at the end of a piece, as for the graphs that bound a disc, and if its boundary ∂D\partial D∂D is a simple closed path. These are the hypotheses of GM 40. The boundary has the positive orientation when DDD lies on its left; for such a region this is the counterclockwise direction. Discs, rectangles and triangles are simple in both directions. Green’s theorem (GM 40) states that ∮∂DP ⁣dx+Q ⁣dy=∬D(∂xQ−∂yP) ⁣dA\oint_{\partial D}P\dd x+Q\dd y=\iint_D(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\dd A∮∂D​Pdx+Qdy=∬D​(∂x​Q−∂y​P)dA when PPP and QQQ are C1C^1C1 on an open set containing D.DD. We need regions with holes as well, which we cut into such pieces.

Definition 17.8 (Admissible region). A compact set D⊂CD\subset\CD⊂C is an admissible region if finitely many segments cut it into regions D1,…,DND_1,\ldots,D_ND1​,…,DN​ that are simple in both directions, such that each part of a cut lies on the boundaries of exactly two pieces, one on each side of it, and such that the parts of the boundaries ∂Dj\partial D_j∂Dj​ that do not lie on a cut make up the boundary ∂D,\partial D∂D, which consists of finitely many simple closed paths. The boundary has the positive orientation when each of them is traversed with DDD on its left: the outer boundary counterclockwise and the boundary of each hole clockwise.

A closed annulus {z∈C:r1≤∣z∣≤r2}\{z\in\C:r_1\le\abs z\le r_2\}{z∈C:r1​≤∣z∣≤r2​} with 0<r1<r20<r_1<r_20<r1​<r2​ is admissible: the two axes cut it into four quarter-annuli, and each of them is simple in both directions. Its positively oriented boundary consists of Cr2(0)C_{r_2}(0)Cr2​​(0) and −Cr1(0).-C_{r_1}(0)−Cr1​​(0). Figure 17.1 below shows two such regions with their cuts.

Lemma 17.9 (Green’s theorem on admissible regions). Let DDD be an admissible region and let PPP and QQQ be real functions that are C1C^1C1 on an open set containing D.DD. Then, with the positive orientation, ∮∂DP ⁣dx+Q ⁣dy=∬D(∂xQ−∂yP) ⁣dA.\oint_{\partial D}P\dd x+Q\dd y=\iint_D(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\dd A .∮∂D​Pdx+Qdy=∬D​(∂x​Q−∂y​P)dA.

Proof. Apply Green’s theorem of GM 40 to each piece DjD_jDj​ with its positive orientation and add the results. The double integrals add up to the double integral over D,DD, since the pieces overlap only along segments (GM 38). Each part of a cut is traversed twice, once by each of the two pieces on its sides, and both pieces keep their own region on the left. Hence the two traversals run in opposite directions, and their contributions cancel. The remaining boundary parts are the parts of ∂D,\partial D∂D, each traversed with DDD on its left. ■

Theorem 17.10 (Cauchy’s theorem). Let fff be analytic on an open set UUU and let f′f'f′ be continuous on U.UU. Then for every admissible region D⊂U,D\subset UD⊂U, ∮∂Df(z) ⁣dz=0,\oint_{\partial D}f(z)\dd z=0 ,∮∂D​f(z)dz=0,(17.7) with the positive orientation of ∂D.\partial D∂D.

Proof. By the Cauchy–Riemann equations of Lecture 15, f′=ux+ivx=vy−iuy.f'=u_x+\iu v_x=v_y-\iu u_yf′=ux​+ivx​=vy​−iuy​. Hence the four partial derivatives of uuu and vvv are, up to sign, the real and imaginary parts of f′.f'f′. They are continuous on U,UU, so uuu and vvv are C1C^1C1 on U.UU. Apply Lemma 17.9 to the two real integrals in (17.2). With P=uP=uP=u and Q=−v,Q=-vQ=−v, ∮∂D(u ⁣dx−v ⁣dy)=∬D(−vx−uy) ⁣dA=0,\oint_{\partial D}(u\dd x-v\dd y)=\iint_D(-v_x-u_y)\dd A=0 ,∮∂D​(udx−vdy)=∬D​(−vx​−uy​)dA=0, and with P=vP=vP=v and Q=u,Q=uQ=u, ∮∂D(v ⁣dx+u ⁣dy)=∬D(ux−vy) ⁣dA=0,\oint_{\partial D}(v\dd x+u\dd y)=\iint_D(u_x-v_y)\dd A=0 ,∮∂D​(vdx+udy)=∬D​(ux​−vy​)dA=0, because both integrands vanish by the Cauchy–Riemann equations. ■

Then ∮∂Tf(z) ⁣dz=0\oint_{\partial T}f(z)\dd z=0∮∂T​f(z)dz=0 for every closed triangle T⊂U,T\subset UT⊂U, and Cauchy’s integral formula (17.8) holds for every closed disc B‾r(z0)⊂U\overline B_r(z_0)\subset UBr​(z0​)⊂U and every z∈Br(z0).z\in B_r(z_0)z∈Br​(z0​).

The sibling course Real and Complex Analysis, whose Lecture nnn we cite as AN nnn (as GM nnn for General Mathematics), proves it: Goursat’s theorem in AN 9 and Cauchy’s integral formula for every analytic function in AN 10, where analytic functions are called holomorphic. The proof of the integral formula uses the triangle result in place of Green’s theorem. The same results are Theorem 1.1 (Goursat’s theorem) and Theorem 4.1 of Chapter 2 of Stein and Shakarchi’s Complex Analysis.

Proposition 17.18 (Analytic functions are infinitely differentiable). Let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv be analytic on an open set U.UU. Then f′f'f′ is analytic on U.UU. Hence fff has complex derivatives of every order on U,UU, and uuu and vvv have continuous partial derivatives of every order. In particular, uuu and vvv are harmonic on U.UU.

Proof. Every z0∈Uz_0\in Uz0​∈U has a closed disc B‾r(z0)⊂U.\overline B_r(z_0)\subset UBr​(z0​)⊂U. By Theorem 17.13, Cauchy’s formula holds on it, and Theorem 17.17 shows that fff has derivatives of every order on Br(z0).B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). Each derivative is complex differentiable, hence continuous.

By the Cauchy–Riemann equations of Lecture 15, ux=Re⁡f′,u_x=\Re f'ux​=Ref′, uy=−Im⁡f′,u_y=-\Im f'uy​=−Imf′, vx=Im⁡f′v_x=\Im f'vx​=Imf′ and vy=Re⁡f′.v_y=\Re f'vy​=Ref′. The same applies to the analytic function f′,f'f′, whose real and imaginary parts are uxu_xux​ and vx.v_xvx​. By induction on k,kk, every partial derivative of order kkk of uuu or vvv is ±Re⁡f(k)\pm\Re f^{(k)}±Ref(k) or ±Im⁡f(k),\pm\Im f^{(k)}±Imf(k), and so it is continuous. In particular uuu and vvv are C2,C^2C2, and the proposition on harmonic parts in Lecture 15 shows that they are harmonic. ■

The proposition removes the hypothesis that uuu and vvv are C2C^2C2 from the statement on harmonic parts in Lecture 15, as announced there. It also shows that every analytic function has a continuous derivative. Hence Cauchy’s theorem, the deformation of a closed path and Cauchy’s integral formula, which assume this continuity, hold for every analytic function.

17.6 When a path meets a singular point

When the integrand is undefined or fails to be continuous at a point of a path, Definition 17.2 does not apply directly, and an ordinary improper integral need not exist. On the real axis the integral ∫−11 ⁣dx/x\int_{-1}^1\dd x/x∫−11​dx/x is an example. As an improper integral it requires the two limits of ∫−1−δ ⁣dx/x=ln⁡δ\int_{-1}^{-\delta}\dd x/x=\ln\delta∫−1−δ​dx/x=lnδ and ∫ε1 ⁣dx/x=−ln⁡ε\int_\varepsilon^1\dd x/x=-\ln\varepsilon∫ε1​dx/x=−lnε as δ→0+\delta\to0^+δ→0+ and ε→0+\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+ separately, and neither limit exists.

Definition 17.21 (Cauchy principal value). Let fff be continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b] except at a point c∈(a,b).c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b). The Cauchy principal value of its integral is pv⁡ ⁣∫abf(x) ⁣dx=lim⁡ε→0+(∫ac−εf(x) ⁣dx+∫c+εbf(x) ⁣dx),\pv\!\int_a^bf(x)\dd x=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\Bigl(\int_a^{c-\varepsilon}f(x)\dd x+\int_{c+\varepsilon}^bf(x)\dd x\Bigr),pv∫ab​f(x)dx=ε→0+lim​(∫ac−ε​f(x)dx+∫c+εb​f(x)dx), when this limit exists.

For f(x)=1/xf(x)=1/xf(x)=1/x on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] the two parts are ln⁡ε\ln\varepsilonlnε and −ln⁡ε,-\ln\varepsilon−lnε, so pv⁡∫−11 ⁣dx/x=0.\pv\int_{-1}^1\dd x/x=0pv∫−11​dx/x=0. The symmetric cutoff is a choice. With the cutoffs ε\varepsilonε on the left and 2ε2\varepsilon2ε on the right the sum is ln⁡ε−ln⁡(2ε)=−ln⁡2\ln\varepsilon-\ln(2\varepsilon)=-\ln2lnε−ln(2ε)=−ln2 for every ε.\varepsilonε. A principal value therefore does not assert that the ordinary improper integral exists. Lecture 20 passes such points on small semicircles and compares ordinary and principal-value integrals.

Summary

A contour integral along a piecewise C1C^1C1 path is a pair of real line integrals. It equals the change of an antiderivative when one exists. The function 1/z1/z1/z has none on the punctured plane, and its integral around the origin is 2πi.2\pi\iu2πi. For an analytic function with a continuous derivative, Green’s theorem and the Cauchy–Riemann equations give Cauchy’s theorem on every admissible region inside an open set on which fff is analytic. Cauchy’s integral formula recovers the values inside a circle from the values on it, and its derivatives give all derivatives of f.ff. With Goursat’s theorem these results hold for every analytic function, which is therefore infinitely differentiable.

  • Contour integral: ∫Cf ⁣dz=∫abf(z(t))z′(t) ⁣dt;\int_Cf\dd z=\int_a^bf(z(t))z'(t)\dd t∫C​fdz=∫ab​f(z(t))z′(t)dt; ∣∫Cf ⁣dz∣≤M L(C);\abs{\int_Cf\dd z}\le M\,L(C)​∫C​fdz​≤ML(C); ∫CF′ ⁣dz=F(zB)−F(zA)\int_CF'\dd z=F(z_B)-F(z_A)∫C​F′dz=F(zB​)−F(zA​) for an antiderivative FFF on an open set containing C.CC.

  • Circle integrals: ∮Cr(z0)(z−z0)n ⁣dz=2πi\oint_{C_r(z_0)}(z-z_0)^n\dd z=2\pi\iu∮Cr​(z0​)​(z−z0​)ndz=2πi for n=−1n=-1n=−1 and 000 for every other integer n;nn; ∮C ⁣dz/(z−z1)=2πi n(C,z1)\oint_C\dd z/(z-z_1)=2\pi\iu\,n(C,z_1)∮C​dz/(z−z1​)=2πin(C,z1​) for a closed path CCC avoiding z1.z_1z1​.

  • Cauchy’s theorem: ∮∂Df ⁣dz=0\oint_{\partial D}f\dd z=0∮∂D​fdz=0 for fff analytic on an open set containing the admissible region D,DD, so paths deform across such regions.

  • Cauchy’s formulas: f(n)(z)=n!2πi∮Cf(ζ)(ζ−z)−n−1 ⁣dζf^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi\iu}\oint_C f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-n-1}\dd\zetaf(n)(z)=2πin!​∮C​f(ζ)(ζ−z)−n−1dζ inside a circle C,CC, for fff analytic on an open set containing the closed disc bounded by C;CC; Cauchy estimates, Liouville’s theorem and the fundamental theorem of algebra follow.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Let CCC be the upper semicircle z(t)=2eitz(t)=2\ee^{\iu t}z(t)=2eit for 0≤t≤π0\le t\le\pi0≤t≤π. Find the imaginary part of ∫Cz‾ ⁣dz\int_C\conj z\dd z∫C​zdz. Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Insert the parametrization into both the integrand and the differential.

On the path, z‾=2e−it\conj z=2\ee^{-\iu t}z=2e−it and z′(t)=2ieitz'(t)=2\iu\ee^{\iu t}z′(t)=2ieit. Their product is 4i4\iu4i. Integrating over the given interval gives 4πi4\pi\iu4πi, so its imaginary part is 4π4\pi4π.

2. The function 1/z1/z1/z is analytic on the annulus 1<∣z∣<31<\abs z<31<∣z∣<3. What does Cauchy’s theorem give for its integral along the positively oriented boundary of 3/2≤∣z∣≤5/23/2\le\abs z\le5/23/2≤∣z∣≤5/2?

Hint. Keep the annular region on the left as you trace each boundary component.

The function is analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed annular region. Its positive boundary traverses the outer circle counterclockwise and the inner circle clockwise, so Cauchy’s theorem gives cancellation. Both circles enclose zero with opposite nonzero winding numbers. Zero lies in the hole, so the hole is allowed and neither circular integral vanishes on its own.

3. Let CCC be the unit circle oriented counterclockwise. What is 12πi∫Cezz3 ⁣dz\frac{1}{2\pi\iu}\int_C\frac{\ee^z}{z^3}\dd z2πi1​∫C​z3ez​dz?

Hint. Match the denominator power with the order of the derivative in Cauchy’s formula.

The denominator power three calls for the second derivative of ez\ee^zez at zero, divided by 2!2!2!. The derivative is 111, so the normalized integral is 1/21/21/2. The value 111 drops the factorial, and 222 multiplies by it. Zero would result from dropping the contribution of the enclosed singular point.

4. Suppose fff is complex differentiable on an open set, with no separate continuity assumption on its first partial derivatives. Which step in the lecture gives the integral formula on small interior circles before higher derivatives have been proved?

Hint. Which version removes the extra regularity needed in the real-variable proof?

The proof by Green’s theorem assumes continuous partial derivatives. The Cauchy–Riemann equations relate their values and provide no such continuity by themselves. The cited result gives Cauchy’s integral formula without that additional assumption. Differentiating the resulting integral then gives the higher derivatives. Starting with the derivative formulas would reverse that reasoning.
